question: to the Commission Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

Audit CT-2025-0037, published on 12 February 2026, found that animal welfare standards are systematically not being met in Chinese slaughterhouses: not a single slaughterhouse using electronic stunning methods had the monitoring equipment which has been required since 2019; in one slaughterhouse, a water bath for stunning designed for two animals was being used for ten at a time; and there was no procedure in place to reject batches in the event of animal welfare violations. Shortcomings in traceability make it impossible to determine whether imported products meet EU standards, allowing non-compliant products to reach the EU market unhindered and at the expense of a level playing field. In the three months between the completion and publication of the report, exports appear to have continued unabated, under a certification system that the Commission itself has already deemed unreliable. 1.

The Commission concludes that the shortcomings are systematic (conclusion 90) and that the certification system does not support the declarations made in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235 (conclusion 106). On what basis have products continued to enter the EU since that finding was made?
What objective criteria does the Commission use to determine when animal welfare guarantees from a third country are inadequate, and at what threshold does this lead to the suspension of imports?

The monitoring equipment, which has been mandatory since 2019, was missing at all the slaughterhouses inspected, without this having been identified in previous audits. How does the Commission explain that this shortcoming went unnoticed for six years?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) In response to the audit and the Commission’s request to ensure compliance, the Chinese competent authority committed to address shortcomings immediately and rapidly, and provided the Commission with an action plan to address the recommendations. The Honourable Member can avail of this action plan at the Commission website1. After assessing the action plan as satisfactory, the Commission services scheduled in the second semester of 2026 an on-site follow up audit to verify the implementation and effectiveness of the proposed actions. The Commission ensures through audits that the exporting country can certify and guarantee the compliance with EU import requirements, or requirements deemed equivalent. When the EU audit identifies non-compliances, the trade partner is requested to produce an action plan containing corrections addressing those non-compliances. The Commission will have to follow up and ensure the good implementation of such corrective actions, including with onsite audits, when appropriate. In case the competent authority fails to provide an adequate action plan, the Commission may take corrective actions, including suspending imports. The previous Commission audit covering poultry meat products and rabbit meat took place in 2017 and did not identify any significant shortcomings concerning animal welfare. The Commission has committed to a 50% increase in the number of audits carried out in third countries which is already reflected in the Director-General for Health and Food Safety audit programme which is publicly available2.
1 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm. 2 Health and food audits and analysis programme https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-
